questions.question: What does it mean for $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n(x)$ to be normally convergent?
options: Each $f_n(x)$ is positive for every $x$.
The numerical series $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.
The functions $f_n$ are all constant functions.
The pointwise limit is always differentiable.

questions.question: If $\|f_n\|_\infty = 2^{-n}$, what can be concluded about $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n(x)$?
options: It cannot converge pointwise.
It is normally convergent.
It is not uniformly convergent.
It is normally convergent only when $X$ is finite.

questions.question: If $\|f_n\|_\infty = \frac{1}{n}$, what does the definition say about normal convergence?
options: The series is normally convergent because $\frac{1}{n}\to 0$.
Normal convergence fails because $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ diverges.
The series is uniformly absolutely convergent for every possible $f_n$.
The series is pointwise divergent at every point.

questions.question: Which implication chain is correct for these convergence notions?
options: Pointwise convergence $\implies$ uniform convergence $\implies$ normal convergence.
Uniform convergence $\implies$ normal convergence $\implies$ pointwise convergence.
Normal convergence $\implies$ uniform absolute convergence $\implies$ uniform convergence $\implies$ pointwise convergence.
Normal convergence $\implies$ pointwise convergence, but it does not imply uniform convergence at all.

questions.question: What does $\|f_n\|_\infty$ measure in normal convergence?
options: The worst-case size of $f_n$ over its domain.
The value of $f_n$ at one single chosen point only.
The derivative of $f_n$.
The number of zeros of $f_n$.

questions.question: For a series of real-valued functions on a common domain $X$, which implication is false in general?
options: Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence.
Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
Uniform absolute convergence implies uniform convergence.
Uniform absolute convergence implies normal convergence.

questions.question: The definition of normal convergence starts from a sequence of bounded functions $f_n$ on a set $X$. Why is the boundedness of each $f_n$ required?
options: So that each $\|f_n\|_\infty$ is finite and $\sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty$ is an ordinary numerical series.
Because bounded terms already guarantee that $\sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.
Because normal convergence is only defined when $X$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
Because an unbounded term $f_n$ would force $\sum_n f_n(x)$ to diverge at every $x\in X$.

questions.question: On a set $X$, let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n}$ for every $x\in X$ and every $n\ge1$ (constant functions). Which statement about $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n$ is correct?
options: It converges uniformly on $X$ but is not normally convergent.
It is normally convergent, because $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n/n$ converges.
It does not converge uniformly on $X$, because $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n$ diverges.
It converges uniformly and absolutely on $X$, because each $f_n$ is constant.

questions.question: For $n\ge1$ let $f_n(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-nx}$ on $X=[0,+\infty)$; each $f_n$ is bounded on $X$. Which convergence question decides whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n$ is normally convergent on $X$?
options: Whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-n}$ converges.
Whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges.
Whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|f_n(x)|$ converges for each $x\in X$.
Whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}n}$ converges.
